anchor_text: <Dialogue speaker="SPEAKER_04" time="22:53">And, uh, You should just make him continue making Lord of Spiritsburg, right? I'm just saying. I have a petition with one signature. All right. It's a start. Just need a little more charisma there, Rory. Um, I'll do my best. What's on your mind?</Dialogue>

<Dialogue speaker="SPEAKER_04" time="01:00:22">Okay, okay. I was a little worried. I read some church fathers saying some bad things about another Marcian. You know, there's a St. Arius as well, by the way. I'll go ahead and say you're my favorite Marcian. Thank you very much, Father. Nice. So what's up, Marcian?</Dialogue>

<Dialogue speaker="SPEAKER_00" time="01:28:58">So on the episode of Apostle Succession, I remember Father D. Young talked about that. He was saying it feels like people don't believe in either [[God]] or life after the resurrection of the dead, because we feel like if somebody dies, they have quote unquote gotten away with it and won't be held accountable. But I think actually a lot of people's reaction to that is more of an attitude of [[Jonah]]. Like, oh, we all know [[God]]'s a big softy, that he's forgiving and merciful. So I think a lot of people can believe in that, but they believe that [[God]] will probably just let it all go. And I think there may be some question out there of like, how does Orthodox see that tension between, you know, mercy and accountability? Like, you know, if I father follow D. Young and he misleads me about which Star Trek captain is best, you know, how would like [[God]] hold him accountable? How would he hold him accountable to that, but still show him mercy and forgiveness?</Dialogue>
